sections.title: Construction Specification Issues
sections.summary: Pavement construction specifications establish minimum requirements for quality; the acceptable level of quality is a surface free of foreign object generators (FOG) that cause foreign object damage (FOD), a critical concern for airfields.
sections.body: Pavement construction specifications provide guidance and establish minimum requirements that, when adhered to, facilitate building a quality pavement. The acceptable level of quality for a rigid airfield pavement comprises desirable surface characteristics and a surface free from foreign object generators (FOG) for the service life of the pavement. FOGs result from distresses in the concrete pavement; a FOG that results in foreign object damage (FOD) is a very critical item for airfield concrete pavements. Good design features, well-developed plans and specifications, and quality construction can minimize or eliminate FOG (and FOD) development. Construction specifications must clearly define the requirements that promote long-term performance of concrete pavement and exclude arbitrary requirements. The Unified Facility Guide Specifications (UFGS) are detailed and cover all aspects of concrete paving, including materials and mixture design issues and required construction techniques and inspection requirements; the specifier and contractor should review military specifications in detail prior to construction.
key_points: Pavement distresses (FOG) that cause foreign object damage (FOD) are a critical airfield concern
Good design, well-developed specifications, and quality construction minimize FOG/FOD
UFGS cover materials, mixture design, construction technique, and inspection requirements
Review military specifications in detail with the contractor before construction begins
sections.applicability: Frames why specification clarity matters most on airfields, where pavement distress becomes a foreign object hazard.

sections.title: Planning Construction Logistics
sections.summary: Successful projects plan logistics in advance, covering grade-control readiness, plant setup/capacity, haul roads, security/access, crew and equipment availability, traffic management, in-pavement structures, inspection/testing, subcontractor readiness, phasing, on-site lab, and fast-track-specific needs; all parties should be included in the communication network.
sections.body: A successful construction project plans all logistical support in advance and pays attention to the smallest details, including: ensuring readiness of all operations (including grade control); concrete plant set-up and traffic flow; concrete plant capacity and production rate; haul road availability and serviceability; security and site access requirements; availability of crews; availability of equipment and materials; construction and airfield traffic management; concrete placement needs (rate of placement); in-pavement structures; acquisition of in-pavement electrical items (affects fast track construction); inspection and testing requirements; subcontractor readiness (crew and equipment availability); project phasing, if any; on-site testing laboratory; and other needs related specifically to fast-track paving. Include all parties involved in a construction project in the communication network. Regardless of project size, pavement construction is a team effort that includes operators and users.
key_points: Logistics planning spans grade-control readiness, plant setup/capacity, haul roads, security, crews/equipment
Fast-track paving has its own logistics needs, including in-pavement electrical item procurement
All parties (contractor, owner, operators, users) should be part of the communication network
sections.applicability: Applies during pre-construction planning to reduce schedule and coordination risk on paving projects.

sections.title: Early Pavement Trafficking
sections.summary: UFGS defines when a pavement may open to construction/design traffic; the default is 14 days (or a demonstrated 400 psi/2.8 MPa flexural strength per ASTM C31/C78) plus 7 days of curing before hauling equipment use, with joints sealed/protected; thicker pavements induce lower construction-traffic stresses.
sections.body: The UFGSs define when a concrete pavement may open to construction traffic and the design aircraft or vehicle traffic. Do not open pavement to aircraft or other design traffic for at least 14 days or longer, depending upon the loading, concrete mixture, and curing conditions. The requirement to allow equipment to operate on the pavement edges is for test specimens molded and cured in accordance with ASTM C31/CRD-C 11, attaining a minimum flexural strength of 400 psi (2.8 MPa) when tested in accordance with ASTM C78/CRD-C 16; absent strength testing, use a 14-day aging requirement. Also complete seven days of curing before allowing hauling equipment to use new concrete, and seal or otherwise protect all joints. Develop specific criteria for typical construction equipment for different concrete pavement thicknesses and for edge and interior loading; for example, for large military facilities with concrete pavement thickness of 16 in. (400 mm) or greater, construction traffic may induce flexural stresses in the range of 100 to 150 psi (700 to 1,000 kPa), while similar equipment may induce higher stresses on thinner (12 in./300 mm or less) pavements. Consider trade-offs between a higher strength requirement and extra thickness for critical areas requiring fast-track construction (e.g., a thicker slab and cement-stabilized base without higher concrete strength versus an asphalt-treated base or granular base with higher-strength concrete). Another consideration for early-age strength is drilling to install dowel bars along the longitudinal joint face of pilot lanes; drilling is typically not initiated until the concrete attains sufficient strength to reduce/eliminate micro-cracking and excess spalling around the drilled holes.
key_points: Minimum opening age: 14 days, or a demonstrated 400 psi (2.8 MPa) flexural strength (ASTM C31/C78/CRD-C 11/16)
Complete 7 days of curing before hauling equipment use; seal/protect all joints first
16-in. (400 mm)+ pavements: construction traffic induces ~100-150 psi (700-1,000 kPa) flexural stress; thinner (<=12 in./300 mm) pavements see higher stress
Fast-track trade-off: thicker slab + stabilized base at normal strength vs. higher-strength concrete on an asphalt-treated/granular base
Drilling for dowel bars along pilot-lane joint faces waits until the concrete is strong enough to resist micro-cracking/spalling around the holes
sections.applicability: Governs when construction and design traffic may be allowed onto new concrete pavement, and how thickness affects the risk.

sections.title: Pre-Bid Meetings
sections.summary: Pre-bid meetings let the owner review project requirements with prospective bidders; besides administrative/contractual matters, they should flag guide-specification modifications, material supply/availability, schedule, and acceptance testing requirements, with minutes distributed to all potential bidders.
sections.body: Pre-bid meetings allow the owner to review project requirements with contractors interested in bidding on a project. Although pre-bid meetings primarily tend to review administrative and contractual matters, it is important to highlight modifications of guide specifications implemented in the plans and specifications, and to address critical material supply and availability issues, the schedule, and specific acceptance testing requirements. It is good practice for contractors to attend pre-bid meetings; distribute meeting minutes to all potential bidders (those requesting bid documents) whether they attend or not. Paving-related discussion items include: owner/contractor organizational hierarchy; value engineering issues; project overview; phasing plan; scheduling criteria and milestones (including which areas are accessible and when, and incentives/disincentives); expected and unexpected delay resolution; alternate bid items; restrictions on site access and working hours; plant and staging area locations; paving sequence for cross-taxiway areas; access/egress and haul road locations and construction traffic control; QA, acceptance testing, and QC requirements; utility connection locations; issuance of design/specification changes; provisions for protecting stabilized layers from freeze conditions; fast-track changes (thicker slab/stiffer base versus higher concrete strength); early age cracking, joint spalling, and edge slump acceptability criteria and corrective-measure guidelines; dowel misalignment testing and resolutions; and test strip construction requirements and acceptance criteria.
key_points: Highlight guide-specification modifications, material supply/availability, schedule, and acceptance testing at pre-bid meetings
Distribute meeting minutes to ALL potential bidders, whether or not they attended
Paving discussion items include dowel misalignment testing/resolution and test strip acceptance criteria
Fast-track trade-offs (thicker slab/stiffer base vs. higher strength) should be raised at this stage
sections.applicability: Applies to the procurement stage, ensuring bidders understand paving-specific requirements before submitting bids.

sections.title: Pre-Award Meetings
sections.summary: Some agencies hold a pre-award meeting, potentially including an on-site survey of the selected contractor's facilities/prior projects, to verify bid representations and capability, and to review contract line items; the contractor may withdraw a bid found to include erroneous pricing.
sections.body: Some agencies hold a pre-award meeting with the selected contractor. As part of these meetings, the contracting officer may perform an on-site survey of the contractor's facilities or previous projects; the survey helps to verify the data and representations submitted with the bid documents and determine if the contractor understands and has overall capabilities to adequately meet the contract requirements. A pre-award meeting is also an opportunity for the contracting officer and contractor to review the contract line items. Based on the discussions with the contracting officer, the contractor has an opportunity to withdraw the bid if it is determined that the bid may have included erroneous pricing.
key_points: Pre-award meetings may include an on-site survey of the contractor's facilities or past projects
Purpose: verify bid representations and contractor capability, and review contract line items
The contractor may withdraw a bid found to contain erroneous pricing at this stage
sections.applicability: Applies between bid selection and contract award, as a capability/pricing verification step.

sections.title: Pre-Construction Meetings
sections.summary: The contracting officer hosts pre-construction meetings reviewing project requirements from Appendix A (logistics, access, security, materials, schedule, inspection/testing, quality management); a dedicated concrete-paving agenda item is the last chance to resolve process issues before equipment mobilizes, and for large projects (>42,000 m2/50,000 yd2) a half-day workshop using this UFC is held.
sections.body: The contracting officer will host pre-construction meetings to review specific project requirements and project planning with the contractor. Review items including issue resolution hierarchy, construction logistics, installation/airfield access and movement, security clearance requirements, the checklist of critical material supply and availability issues, project specifications, approval of materials, schedule, and inspection/testing requirements and the quality management (contractor quality control) plan -- these items are listed in Appendix A. Discuss concrete pavement-related items during the pre-construction meetings as a separate agenda; a concrete paving pre-construction meeting is the last opportunity to discuss concrete paving process issues before equipment starts moving, so that potential problems and solutions can be reviewed by all parties up front. Distribute meeting minutes to all parties. For projects involving more than 42,000 m2 (50,000 yd2) of concrete paving, conduct a half-day concrete pavement construction workshop using this UFC along with project-specific plans and specifications, with attendees including key staff from the contractor's field crew and the testing and inspection crews, to ensure a shared understanding of project requirements. DoD installations or units can fund and schedule the USACE Transportation Systems Center (TSC) to conduct on-site airfield paving workshops and post-award teleconferences, provide on-site technical support during construction, and review PCC mix designs and HMA/WMA job mix formulas, per USACE ER 1110-34-1.
key_points: Review items are listed in Appendix A: logistics, access, security, materials, schedule, inspection/testing, QC plan
A dedicated concrete-paving agenda item is the last chance to resolve process issues before mobilization
Projects > 42,000 m2 (50,000 yd2) require a half-day concrete pavement construction workshop using this UFC
USACE TSC can provide on-site paving workshops, technical support, and mix-design review per ER 1110-34-1
sections.applicability: Applies immediately before construction mobilization to align all parties on paving-specific requirements.

sections.title: Qualifying Construction Materials
sections.summary: State DOT records, third-party accredited labs, or the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center can help qualify materials; alternate materials must still meet specification testing, and aggregate testing lead times (discussed later in the chapter) can be long enough to threaten a ~60-day award-to-start-of-work window.
sections.body: In some localities, the state Department of Transportation (DOT) has information on materials approved for concrete pavement construction; evaluate state DOT records for performance history and certification, which can facilitate the material approval review process. If current independent testing certificates cannot be obtained through material suppliers, DoD installations, units, designers, or contractors may contract with third-party commercial laboratories accredited to perform the required materials testing, or alternatively contract with the U.S. Army Engineering Research and Development Center (ATTN: CEERDC-GM-C, 3909 Halls Ferry Road, Vicksburg, Mississippi, 39180-6199) to qualify a cement or pozzolan for use in DoD pavement construction on a reimbursable basis. Prior to bid solicitation, the design engineer should address material availability and cost; if alternate materials are proposed in lieu of those specified, the contractor must ensure fulfillment of the specification testing requirements. Testing requirements for concrete aggregates may have long lead times, and scheduling conflicts can arise if materials are not pre-qualified in a timely manner; lead times for aggregate testing are discussed later in this chapter.
key_points: State DOT performance-history/certification records can facilitate material approval
Third-party accredited labs, or the U.S. Army ERDC (CEERDC-GM-C), can qualify cement/pozzolan on a reimbursable basis
Alternate materials still must satisfy the full specification testing requirements
Aggregate testing lead times can threaten the typical ~60-day award-to-start-of-work window (see Section 3-8.2)
sections.applicability: Applies to sourcing and pre-qualifying cementitious materials and aggregates before or shortly after award.

sections.title: Evaluation of Local Aggregates
sections.summary: Coarse/fine aggregates must meet ASTM C33/CRD-C 133, but DoD airfields apply an order-of-magnitude-lower deleterious-material limit than ASTM C33 (Tables 3-1/3-2) requiring larger samples; minimum NMA is 38 mm (1.5 in.) with a minimum 10% mass retained on the 25 mm (1 in.) sieve or a #4/#67/fine-aggregate combination, and D-cracking-prone areas warrant a smaller NMA or imported aggregate.
sections.body: The coarse and fine aggregates must meet the requirements of ASTM C33/CRD-C 133; however, for airfield and heavy-duty pavement, additional restrictions and requirements exist. The fineness modulus of the fine aggregate, the limits on deleterious materials, the sample size, and order of testing differ from ASTM C33/CRD-C 133. Limits on deleterious materials are an order of magnitude lower than those in ASTM C33/CRD-C 133 for DoD airfields, so larger samples are required (see Tables 3-1 and 3-2). Key items: the largest maximum aggregate size consistent with placement requirements produces the most economical, least thermally/shrinkage-crack-prone concrete; the minimum nominal maximum aggregate (NMA) size is 38 mm (1.5 in.), and for airfield/heavy-duty pavements the combined gradation must have a minimum of 10 percent mass retained on the 25 mm (1 in.) sieve or be a combination of #4, #67, and fine aggregate; in areas with known D-cracking problems, use a smaller NMA or import aggregate from outside the area; and for roads, aggregates generally need only meet ASTM C33/CRD-C 133 deleterious-material limits, while DoD airfield pavements use limits an order of magnitude lower with additional sample-size/test-sequence requirements.
key_points: Coarse/fine aggregates must meet ASTM C33/CRD-C 133 as a baseline
DoD airfield deleterious-material limits are an order of magnitude lower than ASTM C33 (Tables 3-1, 3-2), requiring larger samples
Minimum NMA is 38 mm (1.5 in.); combined gradation needs >=10% mass retained on the 25 mm (1 in.) sieve, or a #4/#67/fine-aggregate blend
In known D-cracking areas, use a smaller NMA or import aggregate from outside the area
tables: Table 3-2: Deleterious Material Limits in Airfield Aggregates - Percent Mass
sections.applicability: Applies when qualifying coarse and fine aggregate sources for airfield or heavy-duty concrete pavement.

sections.title: Airfield Coarse Aggregate Deleterious Materials Testing Sequence
sections.summary: A 6-step sequential test procedure (minimum sample 90 kg/200 lb for >=19 mm coarse aggregate, 12 kg/25 lb for 4.75-19 mm) washes, then tests and removes clay lumps/friable particles, low-SG chert/cherty stone, lightweight particles, clay-ironstone/shale/claystone family materials, and finally samples for other soft particles.
sections.body: The minimum test sample size of the coarse aggregate is 90 kg (200 pounds) for the 19 mm (3/4 inch) and larger maximum size and 12 kg (25 pounds) for the 4.75 to 19 mm (No. 4 to 3/4 inch) coarse aggregate. Step 1: wash each full sample for material finer than the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve and discard it. Step 2: test the remaining full sample for clay lumps and friable particles and remove them. Step 3: test the remaining full sample for chert and cherty stone with SSD density less than 2.40 specific gravity and remove the lightweight chert/cherty stone, retaining other materials less than 2.40 SG for Step 4. Step 4: test the materials less than 2.40 SG from Step 3 for lightweight particles (Sp. Gr. 2.0) and remove them, restoring the remaining materials less than 2.40 SG to the sample. Step 5: test the remaining sample for clay-ironstone, shale, claystone, mudstone, siltstone, and shaly/argillaceous limestone and remove them. Step 6: test a minimum of one-fifth of the remaining full sample for other soft particles.
key_points: Minimum sample size: 90 kg (200 lb) for coarse aggregate >=19 mm (3/4 in.); 12 kg (25 lb) for 4.75-19 mm (No. 4 to 3/4 in.)
Step 1: wash and discard material finer than 0.075 mm (No. 200 sieve)
Steps 2-5: sequentially test/remove clay lumps and friable particles, low-SG chert/cherty stone, lightweight particles, then clay-ironstone/shale/claystone-family materials
Step 6: test at least one-fifth of the remaining sample for other soft particles
sections.applicability: Applies specifically to airfield coarse aggregate deleterious-material qualification testing.

sections.title: Airfield Fine Aggregate Deleterious Materials Testing Sequence
sections.summary: Minimum fine-aggregate test sample is 5 kg (10 lb) with fineness modulus between 2.50 and 3.40; a 3-step sequence washes fines below the No. 200 sieve, then tests for clay lumps/friable particles and lightweight particles.
sections.body: The minimum test sample size for fine aggregate is 5 kg (10 pounds); the fineness modulus must not be less than 2.50 nor more than 3.40. Step 1: wash each full sample for material finer than the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve and discard it. Step 2: test the remaining full sample for clay lumps and friable particles and remove them. Step 3: test the remaining full sample for lightweight particles (Sp. Gr. 2.0).
key_points: Minimum fine-aggregate sample: 5 kg (10 lb)
Fineness modulus must be within 2.50-3.40
3-step sequence: wash/discard fines below No. 200 sieve, then test for clay lumps/friable particles, then lightweight particles
sections.applicability: Applies specifically to airfield fine aggregate deleterious-material qualification testing.

sections.title: Alkali-Silica Reactivity
sections.summary: ASR susceptibility methodology follows the PCA Guide Specification, but DoD doubles the airfield immersion time to 28 days (vs. 14 for roads) and tightens the expansion limit to 0.08% (vs. 0.1% for roads) to reduce false negatives on slowly reactive materials.
sections.body: Alkali-silica reaction is a deleterious chemical reaction between the reactive silica constituents in the aggregates and alkali in the cement; the product of this reaction can produce significant expansion and cracking of the concrete. The methodology to determine the susceptibility of aggregate to alkali-silica reactivity (ASR) and the effectiveness of mitigation measures is based on the Portland Cement Association's Guide Specification for Concrete Subject to Alkali-Silica Reactions (1998). However, for airfield pavements, DoD doubles the immersion time of the test to 28 days versus the typical 14 days for roads, and sets the expansion limit to 0.08 percent in lieu of 0.1 percent for roads. DoD requires these alterations to reduce the risk of false negative results and ensure deleterious expansion from slowly reactive materials is detected prior to incorporation into DoD airfield pavements.
key_points: ASR susceptibility methodology follows the PCA 1998 Guide Specification for Concrete Subject to ASR
DoD airfield immersion time: 28 days (vs. 14 days for roads)
DoD airfield expansion limit: 0.08% (vs. 0.1% for roads)
Purpose of the tighter DoD criteria: reduce false negatives on slowly reactive aggregates
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating aggregate susceptibility to alkali-silica reaction for airfield vs. road pavement.

sections.title: Service History (Field Performance)
sections.summary: Field performance history is one indicator of ASR susceptibility, but is only sufficient when the current aggregate supply matches historic placements in source, exposure severity (>=15 years), cement content/alkali content/w/cm ratio, and pozzolan class/content/composition.
sections.body: Performance history is a source of information on the susceptibility of an aggregate to ASR. When evaluating a service history as an indicator of the susceptibility of an aggregate to ASR, document that: the current supply of the aggregate is representative of that used in the existing historical placements; the existing historical placements are exposed to the same severity of exposure condition as the proposed placement; the existing historical placements have been exposed to this severity condition for at least 15 years; the existing historical placements have the same cement content with the same alkali content of the cement and a w/cm ratio equal to or greater than the proposed concrete mix; and the existing historical placements have the same pozzolans in both class and content as well as total equivalent alkali content and SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 content. If this information cannot be affirmed and documented, the service history may be insufficient to evaluate the aggregate.
key_points: Service history is only a valid ASR indicator if all five documentation criteria are affirmed
Requires >=15 years of exposure at the same severity as the proposed placement
Requires matching cement content/alkali content, w/cm ratio, and pozzolan class/content/composition
Undocumented service history is treated as insufficient to evaluate the aggregate
sections.applicability: Applies when a designer wants to rely on field performance history instead of (or alongside) laboratory ASR testing.

sections.title: Laboratory Evaluation
sections.summary: Absent adequate service history, or for airfield/heavy-duty paving, both fine and coarse aggregates are tested per ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 (primary screen), C295/CRD-C 127 (petrography), C1293/CRD-C 175 (optional confirmation), and C1567 (mitigation proportioning).
sections.body: In the absence of an adequate history of field performance, or for airfield or other heavy-duty paving, test both fine and coarse aggregates using the methods covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Laboratory ASR evaluation is required absent adequate service history, or always for airfield/heavy-duty paving
Covers both fine and coarse aggregate
sections.applicability: Introduces the laboratory ASR test methods detailed in the following subsections.

sections.title: ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174
sections.summary: For roads, a mean 14-day mortar-bar expansion <=0.10% is acceptable; for military airfield/heavy-duty paving, the limit tightens to 0.08% after 28 days of submersion.
sections.body: For roads, results per this test that yield a mean 14-day mortar bar expansion less than or equal to 0.10 percent indicate acceptable aggregate that may be used for concrete production; when the mean 14-day expansion exceeds 0.10 percent, the aggregate is suspect and additional testing is warranted before approval. For military airfield and heavy-duty paving projects, expansion is limited to 0.08 percent after 28 days of submersion for aggregate to be acceptable without mitigation.
key_points: Roads: acceptable if mean 14-day mortar-bar expansion <= 0.10%
Military airfield/heavy-duty paving: limit is 0.08% after 28 days of submersion (no mitigation)
Exceeding the road limit (0.10%) makes the aggregate suspect and triggers additional testing
sections.applicability: The primary ASR screening test for both road and DoD airfield/heavy-duty aggregate qualification.

sections.title: ASTM C295/CRD-C 127
sections.summary: A petrographic test supplementing ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 that identifies and quantifies reactive mineral constituents, including strained/microcrystalline quartz, chert, opal, and natural volcanic glass in volcanic rocks.
sections.body: This test supplements the results of ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174. This test identifies and quantifies the reactive mineral constituents in the aggregate. Reactive constituents include strained or microcrystalline quartz, chert, opal, and natural volcanic glass in volcanic rocks.
key_points: Petrographic supplement to ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174
Identifies/quantifies reactive constituents: strained/microcrystalline quartz, chert, opal, volcanic glass
sections.applicability: Used alongside ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 to characterize which reactive minerals are present in a suspect aggregate.

sections.title: ASTM C1293/CRD-C 175
sections.summary: An optional confirmation test (concrete prism); a mean one-year expansion exceeding 0.04% indicates potential reactivity, though the long test duration generally makes it impractical for a specific job unless a supplier already has representative results.
sections.body: This is an optional test to verify results of ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174. An aggregate that produces a mean expansion at one year exceeding 0.04 percent is considered potentially reactive. Although the time required for this test generally makes it impractical to use for a specific job, some aggregate suppliers can provide test results specific to their aggregates; the suppliers must demonstrate that the test results represent the aggregate currently being produced from their quarry.
key_points: Optional confirmation test for ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 results
Potentially reactive if mean one-year expansion exceeds 0.04%
Long duration usually makes it impractical for a single job unless a supplier has representative existing results
sections.applicability: Used as an optional, longer-duration confirmation of ASR reactivity, often via pre-existing supplier data.

sections.title: ASTM C1567
sections.summary: Similar to ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 but includes the actual supplementary cementitious materials, used to proportion SCM dosage for ASR mitigation; for airfield paving the acceptance limit is 0.08% expansion after 28 days of submersion.
sections.body: While similar to ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174, this test includes supplementary cementitious materials and is used to determine the proportioning of these supplementary cementitious materials to mitigate ASR. The limits and test length for airfield paving are 0.08 percent after 28 days of submersion for the mitigation to be acceptable.
key_points: Includes the project's actual supplementary cementitious materials in the test
Used to determine SCM proportioning needed to mitigate ASR
Airfield acceptance limit: 0.08% expansion after 28 days of submersion
sections.applicability: Used to verify and proportion a specific SCM mitigation strategy for a reactive aggregate.

sections.title: CRD-C 662
sections.summary: The test method to evaluate lithium nitrate as an ASR mitigation measure, with or without supplementary cementitious materials.
sections.body: If evaluating lithium nitrate as a means to mitigate ASR expansion, with or without supplementary cementitious materials (SCM), test in accordance with CRD-C 662.
key_points: CRD-C 662 governs testing lithium nitrate as an ASR mitigation measure
Applicable whether or not SCMs are also used
sections.applicability: Applies specifically when lithium nitrate is being considered as an ASR mitigation admixture.

sections.title: Mitigation Measures
sections.summary: For roads, a reactive aggregate may still be used with an effective mitigation combination; for military airfields, any combination yielding a mean 28-day ASTM C1567 expansion <=0.08% (using the project's actual cement type/brand) is an acceptable ASR control, typically via low-calcium Class F fly ash, slag, silica fume, or natural pozzolan with portland cement.
sections.body: For roads, if the aggregate demonstrates potential reactivity by ASTM C295/CRD-C 127, ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174, ASTM C1293/CRD-C 175, or by previous field performance, it may be used if an appropriate mitigation measure is effective; specify and test several combinations of cementitious materials to allow the contractor flexibility to meet other project requirements. For military airfield construction, any combination that produces a mean 28-day expansion of 0.08 percent or less when tested according to ASTM C1567 is considered an acceptable method of controlling expansion due to ASR; the cement used for testing must be the same type and brand used on the project. Possible mitigation measures include incorporating a supplementary cementitious material: low-calcium Class F fly ash (CaO content less than 8 percent), slag, silica fume, or natural pozzolan in combination with portland cement.
key_points: Military airfield acceptance: mean 28-day ASTM C1567 expansion <= 0.08%, using the actual project cement type/brand
Effective SCM mitigation options: low-calcium (CaO < 8%) Class F fly ash, slag, silica fume, natural pozzolan
Roads: several cementitious combinations may be specified/tested to give the contractor flexibility
sections.applicability: Applies once an aggregate has demonstrated ASR reactivity and a mitigation strategy must be qualified.

sections.title: D-Cracking
sections.summary: D-cracking is coarse-aggregate disintegration from freeze-thaw saturation cycles, mostly in sedimentary rock; susceptible larger particles should be rejected/beneficiated in freeze-exposed pavements, and unknown-history aggregate is tested per ASTM C666/CRD-C 20 with 350 cycles and a durability index from specimen expansion.
sections.body: D-cracking describes the distress in concrete that results from the disintegration of coarse aggregates after they become saturated and are subjected to repeated cycles of freezing and thawing. For pavements subject to freezing conditions in service, reject or beneficiate aggregate susceptible to D-cracking to remove particles of susceptible size (generally the larger particles). Most rock types associated with D-cracking are of sedimentary origin. If the performance history of a proposed aggregate is unknown and the pavement is subject to numerous freeze cycles during a season, test the aggregate using ASTM C666/CRD-C 20 (Procedure A or B), which tests durability under freeze-thaw cycles in conditions likely to saturate the concrete; modifications for D-cracking testing include increasing the number of cycles to 350 and calculating the durability index from specimen expansion.
key_points: D-cracking: coarse-aggregate disintegration from saturation plus repeated freeze-thaw cycling
Mitigation: reject or beneficiate susceptible (typically larger) particle sizes
Most D-cracking-prone rock types are sedimentary
Unknown-history aggregate in freeze-exposed service: ASTM C666/CRD-C 20, modified to 350 cycles, durability index from expansion
sections.applicability: Applies to freeze-exposed pavements where coarse aggregate durability under repeated saturation/freezing must be verified.

sections.title: Lead Time Required for Aggregate Testing
sections.summary: Table 3-3 gives ASR/freeze-thaw test durations; with only ~60 days typically available from award to start of work, aggregate acceptance testing (per ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174, including mitigation combinations) must be scheduled within, or completed before, that window.
sections.body: Table 3-3 gives the time required for testing of ASR and freeze-thaw (D-cracking). Typically, about 60 days' lead-time is available from contract award to start of work, so aggregate acceptance must be done within that time or before award. Design engineers must specify ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 if ASR testing is required, and must emphasize the test time requirements if aggregate qualification tests are needed; ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 can test the effectiveness of mitigation measures as described in this UFC. Test several combinations of cementitious materials simultaneously to save time and allow flexibility to meet other job requirements.
key_points: Typical award-to-start-of-work window: ~60 days
Test durations by method are in Table 3-3
Design engineers should specify ASTM C1260/CRD-C 174 and flag its time requirements early
Test several cementitious-material combinations simultaneously to save schedule and preserve flexibility
sections.applicability: Applies to schedule planning between contract award and the required start of aggregate-dependent construction work.

sections.title: Availability/Certification of Cementitious Materials
sections.summary: Introduces the certification requirements for portland cement, blended cement, hydraulic cement, and supplementary cementitious materials covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: This section addresses the availability and certification of cementitious materials, covering cement supply security, portland cement types (Table 3-4), blended cement types (Table 3-5), hydraulic cement types (Table 3-6), and supplementary cementitious materials, in the following subsections.
key_points: Covers cement supply, portland cement, blended cement, hydraulic cement, and supplementary cementitious materials
sections.applicability: Introduces the cementitious-materials certification subsections that follow.

sections.title: Cementitious Materials
sections.summary: Secure cement supply for peak construction season; a cement source change requires additional mix design/compatibility testing, since cements with low or poorly-soluble sulfate content can prematurely stiffen with lignosulfonate/triethanolamine water reducers, especially in hot weather.
sections.body: Secure cement supplies to ensure supply during peak construction season. If the cement source is changed, conduct additional mix design and compatibility testing. Problematic combinations often include cements with relatively low sulfate contents or with sulfates available only in forms that are not readily soluble; while such cements may perform satisfactorily alone, they may be prone to early stiffening if used with water-reducing admixtures containing lignosulfonates or triethanolamine, with these effects more pronounced in hot weather. Mixture designs should be pre-qualified using different cementitious materials in the event a substitution is necessary, so that alternate mix design data is available and new materials can be accommodated without delay.
key_points: A cement source change requires additional mix design and compatibility testing
Cements with low/poorly-soluble sulfate content risk early stiffening with lignosulfonate or triethanolamine water reducers
Hot weather amplifies this early-stiffening incompatibility risk
Pre-qualify mixture designs with alternate cementitious materials to avoid delay if substitution becomes necessary
sections.applicability: Applies to securing and pre-qualifying cement supply, and to managing risk when a cement source changes mid-project.

sections.title: Portland Cement
sections.summary: Portland cement types/requirements are per ASTM C150/CRD-C 201 (Table 3-4); do not routinely specify optional alkali/heat-of-hydration limits, since SCM combinations often control ASR and sulfate resistance equally or better than low-alkali or Type II/V cement.
sections.body: The various types and requirements of cement are given in ASTM C150/CRD-C 201; the cement types are presented in Table 3-4. ASTM C150/CRD-C 201 also specifies optional chemical requirements (e.g., maximum alkali content) and optional physical requirements (e.g., heat of hydration) -- specify these judiciously, if at all, since they often increase cost or limit available options, and equally or more effective alternatives frequently exist. For example, deleterious expansions due to ASR may be controlled as well or better by cement combined with Class F fly ash or slag instead of low-alkali cement; generally, do not specify a maximum alkali-content limit, as it may not sufficiently control deleterious expansions, and higher alkali content can even be desirable to speed hydration in cool weather or with SCMs. Sulfate resistance may be obtained with sufficient slag or an appropriate fly ash as well as (or better than) Type II or Type V cement; heat of hydration may be reduced using slag, Class F fly ash, and natural pozzolan combined with portland cement. If cement is used alone (without SCMs), specify the optional requirement for false set, but evaluate the setting characteristics for the concrete.
key_points: Portland cement types (I-V) and requirements: ASTM C150/CRD-C 201, summarized in Table 3-4
Avoid routinely specifying optional alkali-content or heat-of-hydration limits -- SCM combinations often work as well or better
SCM combinations (fly ash, slag, natural pozzolan) can control ASR, sulfate resistance, and heat of hydration
If cement is used without SCMs, consider specifying the optional false-set requirement
tables: Table 3-4: Types and Uses of Portland Cements
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying portland cement type and any optional chemical/physical requirements.

sections.title: Blended Cement
sections.summary: Blended cement types/requirements are per ASTM C595/CRD-C 203 (Table 3-5); ASTM C595 Type I cements match ASTM C150 Type I early-age strength requirements, but actual early strengths trend lower since slag/pozzolans react more slowly, while Type IL(10)/(15) cements (10-15% ground limestone) perform similarly to Type I with slightly more porosity and lower embodied carbon.
sections.body: The types and requirements of blended cements are given in ASTM C595/CRD-C 203; the types are listed in Table 3-5. All cements designated Type I under ASTM C595/CRD-C 203 have comparable strength requirements at early ages as those specified by ASTM C150/CRD-C 201 for Type I cement; however, actual strengths at early ages are generally lower because slag and pozzolans in blended cements react more slowly than cement alone. Type IL(10) and IL(15) cements contain up to 10 or 15 percent limestone ground with the cement clinker; this material provides similar performance to Type I cement but can be slightly more porous, and it has a lower embodied carbon content than similarly produced Type I cement.
key_points: Blended cement types/requirements: ASTM C595/CRD-C 203, summarized in Table 3-5
ASTM C595 Type I matches ASTM C150 Type I early-age requirements on paper, but real early strength trends lower (slower SCM reaction)
Type IL(10)/(15) cements: 10-15% ground limestone, similar performance to Type I, slightly more porous, lower embodied carbon
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying blended cement types for concrete pavement mixtures.

sections.title: Hydraulic Cement
sections.summary: Hydraulic cement types/requirements are per ASTM C1157/CRD-C 271 (Table 3-6), covering general use, high early strength, and moderate/high sulfate resistance and heat-of-hydration designations.
sections.body: The various types of hydraulic cements are given in ASTM C1157/CRD-C 271; the types of hydraulic cements are given in Table 3-6.
key_points: Hydraulic cement types/requirements: ASTM C1157/CRD-C 271, summarized in Table 3-6
Performance-based designations cover general use, high early strength, and moderate/high sulfate resistance and heat of hydration
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying performance-based (ASTM C1157) hydraulic cement types for concrete pavement mixtures.

sections.title: Supplementary Cementitious Materials
sections.summary: SCMs offer improved performance and reduced cost versus specifying ASTM C150 cement alone, including ASR control, reduced permeability, sulfate resistance, and reduced heat of hydration; the following subsections cover pozzolans, dosage, weather effects, ASR performance, and slags.
sections.body: Supplementary cementitious materials offer the potential for improved performance of concrete and reduced cost. They provide benefits more economically and sometimes more effectively than the appropriate choice of ASTM C150/CRD-C 201 cement, including: control of expansions due to ASR; reduced permeability; sulfate resistance; and reduced heat of hydration.
key_points: SCM benefits: ASR control, reduced permeability, sulfate resistance, reduced heat of hydration
Can be more economical and effective than relying on cement type alone
sections.applicability: Introduces the SCM subsections (pozzolans, dosage, weather effects, ASR, slags) that follow.

sections.title: Pozzolans
sections.summary: ASTM C618/CRD-C 255 defines pozzolans; Class F fly ash with SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 > 70%, CaO < 8%, and loss on ignition <= 3% is preferred for ASR control and sulfate resistance, while Class C fly ash is prohibited for concrete pavement.
sections.body: ASTM C618/CRD-C 255 defines pozzolans as siliceous or siliceous-and-aluminous materials that possess little or no cementitious value themselves, but in finely divided form and in the presence of moisture, chemically react with calcium hydroxide at ordinary temperatures to form compounds with cementitious properties. Fly ashes and natural pozzolans must meet ASTM C618/CRD-C 255; Class F fly ash with SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 greater than 70 percent, CaO content less than 8 percent, and loss of ignition not exceeding 3 percent is the preferred choice for controlling ASR and provides sulfate resistance. Class C fly ash is not permitted for concrete pavement.
key_points: Pozzolans per ASTM C618/CRD-C 255: siliceous/aluminous materials reacting with Ca(OH)2 to form cementitious compounds
Preferred Class F fly ash: SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 > 70%, CaO < 8%, loss on ignition <= 3%
Class C fly ash is NOT permitted for concrete pavement
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a fly ash or natural pozzolan source for concrete pavement mixtures.

sections.title: Dosage
sections.summary: Typical Class F fly ash dosage is 15-35% by mass of cementitious material; below 25% replacement SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 must exceed 70%, and at 15% replacement it must exceed 90%.
sections.body: Typical dosages for Class F fly ash are generally between 15 percent and 35 percent by mass of cementitious materials; evaluate sources to determine actual chemical composition and establish typical usage rates. For treatments below 25 percent replacement, the SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 content must be greater than 70 percent; at 15 percent replacement, the SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 content must be greater than 90 percent.
key_points: Typical Class F fly ash dosage: 15-35% by mass of cementitious material
Below 25% replacement: SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 must exceed 70%
At 15% replacement: SiO2+Al2O3+Fe2O3 must exceed 90%
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning Class F fly ash dosage against its chemical composition requirements.

sections.title: Weather Effects
sections.summary: In cool weather, concrete with Class F fly ash may not gain strength quickly enough to allow joint sawing before shrinkage cracks form.
sections.body: In cool weather, concrete with Class F fly ash may not gain strength quickly enough to allow joint sawing before shrinkage cracks form.
key_points: Cool weather risk: slow fly-ash strength gain can miss the joint-sawing window before shrinkage cracking
This risk factors into the hot/cold weather mixture-design decisions discussed in Chapters 7 and 8
sections.applicability: Applies when Class F fly ash mixtures are placed in cool weather where early strength gain governs the sawing window.

sections.title: Alkali-Silica Reactivity
sections.summary: A lower fly ash CaO content is more effective for ASR control (ideally < 8%); for DoD airfields, only Class F fly ash with total equivalent alkali < 4% and (with air-entraining admixtures) loss on ignition <= 3% may be used to mitigate ASR.
sections.body: If fly ash is used to control expansions due to ASR, a lower CaO content is more effective; test the fly ash to verify effectiveness and dosage requirements. Ideally the CaO content should be less than 8 percent. Only use Class F fly ash with a total equivalent alkali content less than 4 percent when mitigating ASR potential in DoD airfield pavement, and only use Class F fly ash with a loss on ignition not exceeding 3 percent when mitigating ASR potential in concrete using air-entraining admixtures in DoD airfield pavement.
key_points: Lower fly ash CaO content (ideally < 8%) is more effective for ASR control
DoD airfield ASR mitigation: Class F fly ash total equivalent alkali content must be < 4%
With air-entraining admixtures on DoD airfields: loss on ignition must be <= 3%
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting/qualifying a fly ash for ASR mitigation specifically on DoD airfield pavement.

sections.title: Mixture Property Control
sections.summary: Natural pozzolans (as Type IP cement components or additives) can be effective at controlling ASR expansion and reducing heat of hydration.
sections.body: Natural pozzolans are available either as components of Type IP cement or as additives. They can be effective in controlling expansions due to ASR and in reducing heat of hydration.
key_points: Natural pozzolans are used either within Type IP cement or as separate additives
Effective for controlling ASR expansion and reducing heat of hydration
sections.applicability: Applies when natural pozzolans are being considered as an ASR/heat-of-hydration control measure.

sections.title: Slags
sections.summary: GGBF slag per ASTM C989/CRD-C 205 comes in three activity-index grades (Table 3-7); typical dosage is 25-50% of cementitious material, with airfields requiring 40-50%, though early-age (up to 28-day) strength trends lower, especially at low temperature or high slag percentage.
sections.body: Finely ground granulated blast furnace (GGBF) slag must meet the requirements of ASTM C989/CRD-C 205; Table 3-7 lists the three grades of GGBF slag, based on their activity index. Typical dosage of slag is between 25 percent and 50 percent of cementitious materials; for airfields, the minimum dose is 40 percent and the maximum is 50 percent. Concrete strength at early ages (up to 28 days) trends lower than cement-only combinations, particularly at low temperatures or at high slag percentages; establish the desired concrete properties while considering the importance of early strengths, curing temperatures, and the properties of the slag, cement, and other concrete materials.
key_points: GGBF slag per ASTM C989/CRD-C 205; three activity-index grades in Table 3-7
Typical slag dosage: 25-50% of cementitious material; airfields require 40-50%
Early-age (<=28-day) strength trends lower with slag, especially at low temperature or high slag percentage
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning GGBF slag dosage for airfield or heavy-duty concrete pavement mixtures.

sections.title: Certification of Admixtures and Curing Compounds
sections.summary: Introduces the certification/use guidance for chemical admixtures and curing compounds covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: This section addresses the certification and appropriate use of chemical admixtures and curing compounds for concrete pavement construction, covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Covers chemical admixture certification/use and curing compound certification/use
sections.applicability: Introduces the admixture and curing-compound subsections that follow.

sections.title: Admixtures
sections.summary: Introduces admixture guidance (general use, air-entraining, accelerating, retarding, water-reducing) covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: Chemical admixtures are ingredients commonly used in paving concrete to obtain or enhance specific properties. This section covers general admixture guidance and the specific categories detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: Covers general admixture guidance plus air-entraining, accelerating, retarding, and water-reducing admixture subsections
sections.applicability: Introduces the admixture-category subsections that follow.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Purchase multi-admixture concrete's admixtures from one manufacturer; obtain dosages via trial batches, never use admixtures to mask marginal mixtures, and ensure admixtures meet ASTM C260/CRD-C 13 (air-entraining) or ASTM C494/CRD-C 87 (Table 3-8 types).
sections.body: Chemical admixtures are ingredients commonly used in paving concrete to obtain or enhance specific properties of concrete. For concrete with multiple admixtures, purchase the admixtures from the same manufacturer; large manufacturers test their own admixtures for incompatibility and can advise on avoiding undesirable reactions. Not all admixtures work well in all applications -- for example, the low slumps typical of paving concrete make certain air-entraining admixtures less effective. Obtain batching requirements, mixing procedures, and recommended dosages from the manufacturer, and use trial batches to determine exact dosages for the particular mixture design; placement temperature affects required dosages, so develop trial batches accordingly. Never use admixtures to compensate for marginal concrete mixtures. Blend admixtures separately into the concrete; do not place admixtures directly on dry aggregate or dry cement, as they can be absorbed and unavailable to mix readily. In higher dosages, some water reducers may retard setting or strength gain. Chemical admixtures must meet ASTM C260/CRD-C 13 (air-entraining admixtures) or ASTM C494/CRD-C 87 (types given in Table 3-8).
key_points: Purchase all admixtures for a multi-admixture mix from the same manufacturer
Determine exact dosages via trial batches; placement temperature affects required dosage
Never use admixtures to compensate for a marginal concrete mixture
Blend admixtures separately into the mix -- do not place directly on dry aggregate or cement
Admixtures must meet ASTM C260/CRD-C 13 (air-entraining) or ASTM C494/CRD-C 87 (Table 3-8 types)
sections.applicability: Applies to general admixture selection, sourcing, and batching practice.

sections.title: Air-Entraining Admixtures
sections.summary: Air-entraining admixtures protect freeze-exposed concrete and can improve fresh workability (reduced water demand, bleeding, segregation), but higher air content reduces strength -- typically ~5% strength loss per 1% air increase.
sections.body: Air-entraining admixtures entrain a system of finely divided air bubbles in the cement paste; they are an essential protection for concrete exposed to freezing, providing outlets for freezing water to expand without disrupting the internal structure. Air-entraining admixtures can also improve the workability of fresh concrete, reducing water demand, bleeding, and segregation. Select an admixture appropriate for pavement use, since some admixtures are used only in concretes with higher slump allowances than typical for airfield pavements. Higher air content in concrete reduces its strength; if the air content of production concrete is higher than specified in the approved mix design, it may reduce the strength of in-place concrete and strength samples. Typically, a 1 percent increase in air results in a 5 percent loss in compressive strength.
key_points: Essential freeze protection: entrained air bubbles absorb the expansion of freezing water
Also improves fresh workability: reduces water demand, bleeding, segregation
Rule of thumb: 1% increase in air content -> ~5% loss in compressive strength
Choose an admixture suited to typically-low pavement slumps
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and controlling air-entraining admixture dosage for freeze protection and workability.

sections.title: Accelerating Admixtures
sections.summary: Type C/E accelerating admixtures speed setting and early strength gain, mainly for cold weather or repairs; later-age strength may decrease and durability may suffer, so alternate means (Type III cement, more cement, heating, better curing) are often preferable.
sections.body: Accelerating admixtures are classified as Type C and Type E by ASTM C494/CRD-C 87; they accelerate the setting and early strength gain of concrete. Typically, they are used only in cold weather or in repairs when reducing setting time by an hour or two is important, or when some increase in early-age strength is needed. If any of these properties are needed over the course of the job, it is preferable to design the concrete accordingly rather than rely on accelerating admixtures. Accelerating admixtures primarily affect setting time, heat evolution, and strength development; later-age strength may decrease, and in aggressive environments durability may be adversely affected. Alternate means of obtaining early strength development include use of Type III cement, higher cement contents, heating the water or aggregates, improving curing and protection, or some combination.
key_points: Type C/E accelerating admixtures per ASTM C494/CRD-C 87 speed setting and early strength gain
Best suited to cold weather or repairs needing an hour-or-two reduction in setting time
Later-age strength may decrease; durability may suffer in aggressive environments
Alternatives: Type III cement, higher cement content, heated water/aggregates, improved curing
sections.applicability: Applies when early-age strength or reduced setting time is needed, especially in cold weather or repair work.

sections.title: Retarding Admixtures
sections.summary: Retarding admixtures delay initial/final set (affecting strength gain for 1-7 days depending on dosage) without slowing slump loss, useful in hot weather/long hauls, but overdosing in hot weather can retard so much that drying cracking precedes sawable strength.
sections.body: Retarding admixtures delay the initial and final setting times; however, they do not reduce the rate of slump loss. They affect the rate of strength gain for as little as one or two days, or as long as seven days, depending on the dosage; they may be used in hot weather when long haul times are unavoidable or to prevent the formation of cold joints. Changes in temperature may require dosage adjustments to maintain the desired setting time; in hot weather, dosage may be increased to the point where excessive retardation occurs, which in some cases results in cracking because the concrete begins to crack from drying before gaining sufficient strength to saw the joints.
key_points: Delays initial/final set (1-7 days effect on strength gain, dosage-dependent); does NOT slow slump loss
Used in hot weather for long haul times, or to prevent cold joints
Overdosing in hot weather can retard set enough that drying cracking precedes sawable strength
sections.applicability: Applies to hot-weather placements with long haul times, or where cold-joint prevention is needed.

sections.title: Water-Reducing Admixtures
sections.summary: Types A, D, E (ASTM C494/CRD-C 87) reduce w/c ratio, increase workability, or reduce water/cement content for a given workability; Type A can behave as Type D at higher dosages, and high-range water reducers are typically not used in pavement concrete.
sections.body: Water-reducing admixtures, as defined in ASTM C494/CRD-C 87 as Types A, D, and E, are used in concrete pavement applications. Some Type A water-reducing admixtures act as Type D (water-reducing and retarding) admixtures at higher dosages; high amounts of water-reducing admixtures may lead to excessive retardation, and the rate of slump loss is increased when using water-reducing admixtures. Some water-reducing admixtures enhance the effectiveness of air-entraining admixtures, so a lower dosage achieves the required air content. High-range water reducers are typically not used in pavement concrete. Types A, D, and E can be used to reduce the water/cement ratio at a given workability, increase workability for a given water content, or reduce water and cement contents for a given workability.
key_points: Types A, D, E (ASTM C494/CRD-C 87) used in pavement concrete; Type A can act as Type D at higher dosage
High dosages increase retardation and slump-loss rate
Can enhance air-entraining admixture effectiveness, allowing a lower AEA dosage
High-range water reducers are typically not used in pavement concrete
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a water-reducing admixture type/dosage for pavement concrete workability and strength control.

sections.title: Curing Compounds
sections.summary: Curing compounds must conform to ASTM C309/CRD-C 304 and CRD-C 300 (efficiency per ASTM C156/CRD-C 306); pigmented (white, in hot/sunny conditions) compounds are recommended, and must maintain >=80% surface relative humidity for 7 days without sagging or running.
sections.body: Curing compounds (liquid membrane-forming compounds) need to conform to the requirements of ASTM C309/CRD-C 304 and CRD-C 300, as applicable; ASTM C156/CRD-C 306 specifies a method for determining the efficiency of curing compounds, waterproof paper, and plastic sheeting. Pigmented curing compounds are recommended because they make it easy to verify proper application; for concrete placement on sunny days and in hot weather, the selected curing compound should contain a white pigment to reflect the sun's heat. Properly applied curing compounds must maintain the relative humidity of the concrete surface above 80 percent for seven days; be uniform and easily maintained in a thoroughly mixed solution; not sag, run off peaks, or collect in grooves; and form a tough film to withstand early construction traffic.
key_points: Curing compounds: ASTM C309/CRD-C 304 and CRD-C 300; efficiency per ASTM C156/CRD-C 306
White-pigmented compounds recommended for sunny/hot-weather placements
Must maintain surface relative humidity above 80% for 7 days
Must not sag, run off peaks, or collect in grooves, and must resist early construction traffic
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and specifying curing compounds for concrete pavement curing.

sections.title: Quality Control/Quality Assurance Requirements
sections.summary: Introduces CQC/QA specification development (implementation is in Chapter 10), covering basic definitions, general issues, the CQC plan, its review, and CQC-vs-QA responsibilities in the following subsections.
sections.body: The development of specifications for contractor quality control/quality assurance (CQC/QA) is discussed in this section; the implementation of specific project CQC/QA requirements is discussed in Chapter 10.
key_points: This section covers CQC/QA specification development; Chapter 10 covers implementation
Subsections: basic definitions, general issues, CQC plan content, CQC plan review, CQC-vs-QA responsibilities
sections.applicability: Introduces the CQC/QA subsections that follow, and cross-references Chapter 10 for implementation.

sections.title: Basic CQC/QA Definitions
sections.summary: Introduces the definitions of Contractor Quality Control, Quality Assurance, and Acceptance Testing covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: This subsection defines the basic CQC/QA terms used throughout the chapter: Contractor Quality Control (CQC), Quality Assurance (QA), and Acceptance Testing.
key_points: Defines CQC, QA, and Acceptance Testing as used throughout the chapter
sections.applicability: Introduces the CQC/QA/Acceptance Testing definition subsections that follow.

sections.title: Contractor Quality Control (CQC)
sections.summary: CQC (process control) covers the contractor's roles/responsibilities: testing, monitoring, and reporting to document specification compliance and allow timely process adjustments; requires a written CQC plan approved by the Contracting Officer.
sections.body: CQC, also called process control, refers to the contractor's roles and responsibilities. The goal of the CQC program is to provide testing, monitoring, and reporting of information to adequately document that the contractor is meeting the project specifications and to allow the contractor to make timely adjustments to the construction process. The contractor needs to develop a written CQC plan that is available for review and approved by the Contracting Officer.
key_points: CQC = process control = the contractor's roles/responsibilities
Goal: document specification compliance and enable timely construction-process adjustments
Requires a written CQC plan, reviewed and approved by the Contracting Officer
sections.applicability: Defines the contractor's quality-control role and the written CQC plan requirement.

sections.title: Quality Assurance (QA)
sections.summary: QA covers the government's roles/responsibilities: all actions needed to give reasonable confidence the final product meets government intent for serviceability/maintenance, verifying the contractor's CQC results are representative and that the contractor is 'doing the right things'.
sections.body: QA consists of all actions necessary to provide a reasonable level of confidence that the final product will meet the intent of the government from a serviceability and maintenance perspective; QA refers to the government's roles and responsibilities. The goal of the QA program is to verify that the results from the contractor's CQC plan are truly representative of the actual material being placed and that the contractor is 'doing the right things.' The government will develop a written QA plan and distribute it to all project personnel, including the contractor.
key_points: QA = the government's roles/responsibilities, verifying the contractor's CQC results are representative
Goal: confidence the final product meets government serviceability/maintenance intent
The government develops a written QA plan and distributes it to all project personnel
sections.applicability: Defines the government's quality-assurance role, distinct from the contractor's CQC role.

sections.title: Acceptance Testing
sections.summary: Acceptance testing determines compliance with contract requirements and links to pay items; it can be part of QA, CQC, or both, so responsibilities (e.g., who fabricates/field-cures vs. transports/tests specimens) must be clearly defined before work starts.
sections.body: Acceptance testing describes the QA tests conducted to determine the degree of compliance with contract requirements and is linked to pay items; acceptance testing can be part of the QA or CQC plan or both. For example, CQC may be responsible for fabricating and field curing concrete strength samples, but QA is responsible for transporting, laboratory curing, and testing. Clearly define all acceptance testing procedures and responsibilities prior to starting any work.
key_points: Acceptance testing determines contract compliance and is linked to pay items
Can sit within the QA plan, the CQC plan, or be split between them
All acceptance-testing procedures/responsibilities must be clearly defined before work starts
sections.applicability: Applies to defining who performs and is responsible for pay-linked acceptance testing on a project.

sections.title: General Issues
sections.summary: Key quality-related items include testing crew/lab/plant certification, test equipment calibration, QA/QC conflict resolution, control chart use, and timely CQC plan development, data management, and decision-making.
sections.body: Important quality-related concrete pavement construction items include: testing crew training/certification (typically ACI certification); testing laboratory certification (per ASTM C1077/CRD-C 553); plant certification; plant operator certification; test equipment calibration (flexural strength test machine and other laboratory equipment); the role of QA/acceptance or verification and resolution of conflicts between QA and QC test results; use of control charts by contractors; development of a CQC plan; management of CQC data; timely review and processing of CQC data; and the construction team's ability to make decisions quickly with changing project conditions.
key_points: Testing crew (typically ACI-certified), testing laboratory (ASTM C1077/CRD-C 553), plant, and plant operator certification
Test equipment calibration, including the flexural strength test machine
Process for resolving conflicts between QA and QC test results
Timely CQC data management and quick project decision-making
sections.applicability: Serves as a checklist of general quality-program items to address before/during construction.

sections.title: CQC Plan
sections.summary: A comprehensive CQC plan is essential; pre-construction CQC/QA meetings resolve conflicts/gaps, and a good plan's components run from introduction/organization through inspections, testing schedules, deficiency reporting, conflict resolution, and appendices.
sections.body: One of the most important activities of a concrete pavement construction project is the contractor's development of a comprehensive CQC plan, which the contractor must implement and adhere to throughout construction. Meetings between the CQC and QA representatives prior to construction help resolve conflicts and identify gaps in the inspection process. The components of a good CQC plan include: an introduction (project description, key contacts, plans/specs highlights); the purpose of CQC; an organization chart (chain of responsibility); duties and responsibilities (QC manager, QA/acceptance testing administrator, project engineers, technicians/inspectors); inspections (tests required, frequency, acceptance criteria, covering material, excavation/embankment, concrete paving, and demolition inspection); QC test schedules/testing plans and report submittals; deficiencies reporting; conflict resolution; changes to the CQC/supplemental items; a placement agreement form; and appendices as needed.
key_points: Pre-construction CQC/QA meetings resolve conflicts and identify inspection-process gaps
CQC plan components: introduction, purpose, org chart, duties/responsibilities, inspections (tests/frequency/acceptance criteria)
Also includes: test schedules, deficiency reporting, conflict resolution, change process, placement agreement form
sections.applicability: Defines the required content/structure of a contractor's CQC plan for a concrete pavement project.

sections.title: Review of CQC Plan
sections.summary: Write the CQC plan clearly and review it for ambiguity in sampling locations, test counts/procedures, special provisions, and acceptance limits; management support is essential, and Appendix B provides the inspection/testing checklist to help review.
sections.body: Write the CQC plan clearly to minimize any misunderstanding. Review the plan for ambiguity with respect to sampling locations, number of tests, test procedures, special provisions, and acceptance limits; make copies of all test procedures cited in the plan readily available at the project site or test facility. The management of each organization must fully support the CQC process, since without management support urgent deadlines and outside pressures can dominate project activities and CQC testing/inspection will suffer. An inspection and testing checklist is provided in Appendix B. Review CQC plans for: whether all required tests are discussed and properly standards-referenced; whether testing requirements/procedures are clearly defined; what items are tested; what actions follow unacceptable/out-of-limit results; documentation procedures/timelines; how results are reported; how nonconforming results are handled; hot/cold weather and nighttime construction procedures; and the chain of command for decision making.
key_points: Review for ambiguity in sampling locations, test counts, procedures, special provisions, acceptance limits
Management support is essential -- without it, CQC testing and inspection suffer under schedule pressure
Appendix B provides the inspection and testing checklist to support this review
Confirm hot/cold weather and nighttime construction procedures and the decision-making chain of command are addressed
sections.applicability: Applies when the government/QA reviews a contractor-submitted CQC plan for completeness before approval.

sections.title: CQC Versus QA Testing Responsibilities
sections.summary: QA testing drives acceptance/pay adjustments while contractor CQC testing drives process control, which can create conflicts; timely communication and joint review after plan approval resolve gaps, and CQC data management (results, consignment forms, control charts, RFIs) should be tracked so nothing is missing at project end.
sections.body: Contractors and inspectors must be aware of testing requirements and how test results are used: QA testing is used for acceptance and pay adjustments, while the contractor's test results are used for process control, which can create conflicting situations. Minimize the potential for conflicts between QA and QC through timely communications; once the CQC and QA plans are created, reviewed, and approved, the contractor and inspection teams should meet to review and resolve any potential conflicts or gaps (e.g., the CQC plan may assume the owner makes flexural strength samples for opening to traffic while the QA plan assumes it is the contractor's responsibility, or storage-location assumptions may differ). An often-overlooked part of any project is CQC data management, which includes test results and procedures, consignment forms, laboratory control charts, and requests for information; track any missing information and resolve it as soon as possible, since missing items are difficult to locate if the project team waits until the end of the project. The schedule for submission and the review process must be determined before construction begins.
key_points: QA testing drives acceptance/pay adjustments; contractor CQC testing drives process control -- a source of potential conflict
Contractor and inspection teams should jointly review CQC/QA plans after approval to resolve gaps
CQC data management includes test results, consignment forms, control charts, and RFIs -- track missing items promptly
Determine the document submission schedule and review process before construction begins
sections.applicability: Applies to reconciling CQC and QA roles and to managing CQC documentation through the life of the project.

sections.title: Test Section Construction
sections.summary: Test sections are mandatory for design-build, all airfield, and other slipform projects >=250 mm (10 in.) thick, to evaluate batching/transporting/placement/finishing/curing; both contractor and government senior representatives must attend since it establishes acceptable/unacceptable procedures.
sections.body: Test sections are mandatory for all design-build paving projects, all airfield paving projects, and for other paving projects where the pavement thickness is 250 mm (10 in.) or greater and constructed using slipform paving. The designer and using agency decide where the test section will be constructed, and use it to evaluate concrete batching, transporting, placement, finishing, and curing processes. The specification clearly identifies the objectives for test section construction and establishes the construction monitoring and acceptance plan requirements; develop the acceptance plan in accordance with project requirements, and clearly define test section dimensions and construction location. The designer and using agency must decide whether to place the test section near the project site or allow its use as part of the final pavement (provided it is at an outer edge location). Both the contractor and government must have senior representatives present during test section placement, as this event establishes the acceptable and unacceptable procedures; the government must give the contractor timely notification of acceptance or a clear explanation of what is rejected.
key_points: Mandatory for: all design-build paving, all airfield paving, and other slipform projects >=250 mm (10 in.) thick
Used to evaluate batching, transporting, placement, finishing, and curing processes
Senior representatives from both contractor and government must attend -- it sets acceptable/unacceptable procedures
Government must give timely acceptance notification or clear rejection explanation
sections.applicability: Applies whenever test section construction is required (design-build, airfield, or thick slipform projects).

sections.title: Test Section Details
sections.summary: Test sections should use the anticipated paving width, run ~122 m (400 ft), replicate anticipated conditions/equipment/haulers, include blockouts, at least one construction header, tie-down/ground points if used, and hand placement on large projects.
sections.body: Consider including the following construction details in the test section: pave at the paving width anticipated for the project; allow sufficient length (typically 122 m [400 ft]) for the contractor to demonstrate their paving operation; place in conditions anticipated during pavement construction; use the same equipment and concrete haulers as used during construction; include blockouts to evaluate paving processes where light cans and embedded steel are located; include at least one construction header to evaluate starting and ending; include tie-down (mooring point) and ground point if the paving project includes them; and for large projects, test strip construction should also include hand placement.
key_points: Pave at the anticipated project width, typically 122 m (400 ft) long
Use the same conditions, equipment, and concrete haulers as production paving
Include blockouts (light cans/embedded steel), at least one construction header, and any tie-down/ground points
Large projects should also test hand placement in the test strip
sections.applicability: Applies to designing/laying out a test section so it exercises the same conditions as production paving.

sections.title: Test Evaluation Items
sections.summary: Test sections are built with the same procedures as production paving; the following subsections list items to evaluate at each stage: pre-paving inspection, batch plant, delivery, placement, QA/QC, consolidation/finishing, texturing, curing, sawcutting, acceptance, and post-construction adjustments.
sections.body: Construct test sections using the same procedures as for production paving. The following subsections contain the items to evaluate during test section placement, spanning pre-paving preparation, batch plant operations, concrete delivery, placement, QA/QC, consolidation and finishing, texturing, curing, sawcutting, final acceptance, and any resulting adjustments to QC/QA operations.
key_points: Test sections are built using the same procedures as production paving
Evaluation spans the full process: pre-paving prep through sawcutting and final acceptance
sections.applicability: Introduces the test-evaluation-item subsections that follow.

sections.title: Pre-Paving Preparation and Inspection Activities
sections.summary: Prior to paving, verify base condition/grade controls, joint locations, dowel bar baskets/embedded steel/tie bars, blockouts, aggregate gradation/moisture, transport/placement/consolidation/finishing/texturing/curing equipment, and paver vibrator frequency/amplitude.
sections.body: Accomplish the following activities prior to starting paving operations: base condition (grade and surface); grade controls (stringline setup, paver track-line); joint locations; dowel bar baskets, embedded steel, and tie bars, if used; blockouts; concrete aggregate (for gradation and moisture content); equipment for transporting, placing, consolidating, finishing, texturing, and curing; and vibrators on pavers (for frequency and amplitude).
key_points: Verify base condition, grade controls, joint locations, and dowel/steel/tie-bar placement before paving
Verify blockouts, aggregate gradation/moisture, and all process equipment
Check paver vibrator frequency and amplitude before starting
sections.applicability: Applies to the pre-paving inspection checklist ahead of test section (and, by extension, production) paving.

sections.title: Batch Plant Operations
sections.summary: Introduces the plant production rate and concrete uniformity evaluation items covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: Evaluate the following batch plant charging and concrete mixing processes prior to the start of paving operations.
key_points: Covers plant production rate and concrete uniformity checks before paving starts
sections.applicability: Introduces the batch plant operation subsections that follow.

sections.title: Plant Production Rate
sections.summary: Batching at expected production rates evaluates whether additional loaders are needed and whether stockpile management plans are acceptable; mixing times are established and approved based on plant uniformity testing.
sections.body: Batching through the plant at expected production rates will evaluate whether additional loaders are required and stockpile management plans are acceptable. Establish and approve mixing times based on plant uniformity testing.
